never: Uses 'very' or 'really' as intensifiers
Uses adverbs ending in '-ly' to modify dialogue tags (never 'she said softly')
Uses question marks on rhetorical or elegiac questions ('Where did she go, that girl' has no question mark)
Uses exclamation points
Uses italics for emphasis within prose sentences
Uses em-dashes for interruption or aside
Uses dialogue tags other than 'said' or none at all
Uses the word 'beautiful' to describe anything emotional or spiritual
Uses similes with 'like' in a casual or decorative way — similes are always load-bearing and extended
Uses passive constructions to avoid assigning agency when agency is the moral point
Uses 'suddenly' or 'immediately' as temporal markers
Uses paragraph breaks to signal mere topic change — breaks are structural and rhythmic, not organizational
Uses the word 'feel' or 'felt' to name an emotion directly without embodying it
Uses abstract nouns like 'freedom' or 'justice' without immediately grounding them in a physical or communal act
Uses third-person omniscient to explain or editorialize — the narrator witnesses, does not adjudicate
Uses conventional flashback signaling ('she remembered that day when...')
Uses the word 'perhaps' or 'maybe' to hedge narrative assertion
Uses comic relief or irony to deflate grief
Uses a sentence of more than three clauses without a rhythmic payoff at the end
Uses 'and then' as a sequential connector in narrative prose
always: Ends a paragraph on a short, syntactically simple sentence after a long accumulating one
Repeats a key verb or phrase in immediate succession for incantatory effect ('It rose. It rose in the cornbread')
Opens a new paragraph with a single proper noun or a single concrete sensory word set off alone
Uses the second person 'you' to suddenly implicate the reader inside a third-person narrative
Embeds a corrective or counter-statement within a sentence using 'or' to revise what was just said ('or the mother was tired, or the mother had simply not been loved')
Assigns physical geography or weight to abstract conditions ('Love is getting up in the dark')
Uses the present tense for statements of communal or historical truth inside otherwise past-tense narrative
Gives the dead grammatical equality with the living — they act, wait, remember, speak
Uses anaphora ('She gave. She gave until') to build toward a single devastating clause
Names women by first name only, restoring individuality the historical record denied
Uses free indirect discourse so that a character's logic becomes indistinguishable from the narrator's for exactly one sentence before pulling back
Introduces a character's defining trait through what their hands know or have done
Places the moral or thematic statement of a passage in a subordinate clause, not the main clause
Uses lists of three concrete nouns or images before making an abstraction ('the placentas and the milk teeth and the names whispered into mason jars')
Ends a long syntactic sequence with a monosyllabic or two-syllable word that closes like a door
Uses community voice ('the women said,' 'the old folks said') as a chorus that is simultaneously wise and complicit
Converts an adjective into a noun to make the quality a thing that can be owned, carried, or lost ('the burning,' 'the keeping,' 'the breaking')
Uses the word 'and' to begin sentences when accumulation must not pause for subordination
Anchors spiritual or supernatural events in a specific, mundane sensory detail to refuse the reader the distance of allegory
Structures a paragraph as a question the community cannot answer followed by the answer the individual woman already knows
